title: The Radio: Bells, Gunpowder and Invisible Waves

beats.say: In eighteen ninety five, in a college in Calcutta, a professor rang a bell in another room. No wire. Through two walls.
He even set off gunpowder the same way.
His name was Jagadish Chandra Bose. And the trick he used is the same one inside every radio.
Before this, a message needed a wire, like the telegraph.
Then, in eighteen sixty five, James Clerk Maxwell predicted invisible waves of electricity and magnetism, travelling at the speed of light.
In eighteen eighty six, Heinrich Hertz in Germany made those waves with a spark, and caught them across the room.
Bose used tiny waves, sixty gigahertz, and sent them twenty three metres, through two walls.
Marconi filed his wireless patent in eighteen ninety six. In nineteen oh one, he reported hearing a signal across the Atlantic.
So how does a radio work? A transmitter pushes electrons back and forth in an antenna, very fast. That sends out a wave.
The wave crosses space at the speed of light, and nudges the electrons in your radio's antenna.
Tuning picks just one wave. AM changes the wave's strength. FM changes its frequency.
Here's the part nobody tells you. Radio has no single inventor. Maxwell, Hertz, Bose, Marconi and others each built a piece.
In India, the Radio Club of Bombay went on air in nineteen twenty three. All India Radio got its name in nineteen thirty six.
Today its signal covers about ninety nine percent of Indians. But only about five in every hundred homes still own a radio set.
